catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agnetz: Agnetz, from Latin agnus, lamb, is the Slavonic word for the square bread portion cut from the first loaf when preparing for Mass according to the Greek rite. That preparation is called the proskomide. The word is used in Byzantine Catholic and Greek Orthodox churches in the United States as well as Europe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexander-max:
Alexander Maximilian Seitz was a German painter, born at Munich in 1811 and dead at Rome in 1888. Cornelius taught him; Joseph Sold by His Brethren and the Seven Sleepers, two early pictures, won quick recognition. Heinrich Hess gave him work on the All Saints frescoes. After he painted four of the sacraments, Cornelius brought him to Rome, where he found a kindred spirit in Overbeck.

Seitz helped Overbeck with the frescoes of the Evangelists and Apostles at Castel Gandolfo and, with his gifted son Ludwig, later completed Overbeck's frescoes at Diakovár cathedral. With his son he also painted a cycle of saints for Herder of Freiburg. Besides scenes of Roman common life, he treated chiefly Old and New Testament subjects. These included the Adoration of the Shepherds, Christ as the Friend of Children, and the Finding of Moses, all in Overbeck's spirit.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amalarius-of-:
Amalarius of Metz, liturgical writer born at Metz late in the eighth century, died about 850. Long thought distinct from Amalarius of Trèves, he is now held to have become Bishop of Trèves about 811, by Dom Morin's researches. He left after two years as envoy to Constantinople. Alcuin's disciple, he later attended synods at Aix-la-Chapelle and Paris.

He served Louis le Débonnaire as ambassador to Gregory IV, and governed Lyons during Agobard's exile, where Florus opposed his antiphonary. Censured at Quierzy in 838 over the divided Host, later drawn into Gottschalk's predestination controversies, he wrote on liturgy. His De ecclesiasticis officiis explains Mass, Office, benedictions, ordinations, vestments, seasons from Septuagesima to Pentecost, and Holy Week. His De ordine antiphonarii explains the Office's arrangement and the antiphons' origin, and defends his compilation from Rome's and Metz's antiphonaries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cardinal-de-r:
Cardinal de Retz, Archbishop of Paris, was born at the Château of Montmirail in October 1614 and died in Paris in August 1679. Destined for the Church though he said it suited neither his taste nor his temper, he learned seven languages. Reading Plutarch and Sallust gave him a taste for republican maxims and conspiracy. At eighteen he wrote on the conspiracy of Fieschi, approving what his model Mascardi had blamed.

After plots against Richelieu and consecration as coadjutor in 1644, he won Paris by sermons and reform of priests, then opposed Mazarin through the Fronde years. Arrested by Louis XIV's order in December 1652, he later resigned the see in 1662 for the Abbey of St. Denis, whose income doubled the archbishopric's. He figured in the conclaves that chose Clement IX and Clement X, and his memoirs, begun in 1671, first appeared in 1717.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cesar-mansuet:
César-Mansuete Despretz was a chemist and physicist born at Lessines, Belgium, on 11 May 1798 and dying at Paris on 11 May 1863. Early in life he became master of studies at the Bruges lyceum, then went to Paris, where Gay-Lussac had him made tutor of the chemical course at the Ecole Polytechnique. In 1824 he became professor of physics at the Collège Henri IV, and in 1837 took the physics chair at the Sorbonne.

Naturalized French in 1838, he entered the Academy of Sciences in 1841 as successor of Savart. His researches helped lay the foundations of modern physics, above all in heat. He studied latent heat in 1818 and heat conduction in 1821. An Academy-crowned memoir on animal heat followed in 1822, then liquid compressibility in 1823 and gas density in 1827, which showed Mariotte's law did not hold exactly for gases. He died a devout Catholic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eugene-muentz:
Eugene Muentz was a French savant and historian, born at Soulz-sous-Forêts, near Mülhausen, Alsace, on 11 June 1845 and dead at Paris on 2 November 1902. He studied law, but turned to the Revue Alsacienne, where his articles caused much comment. Just then attention was being directed in France to the study of history. Albert Dumont founded the École Française at Rome, and Müntz became one of its pupils.

Louis Duchesne, director of the school, was a fellow-student. Müntz explored the Vatican Archives and Library, amassing the erudition he revealed in later years. From that time he devoted himself to unravelling the history of art in Italy. About 1880, with Morelli and Milanesi, he contributed immensely to this study, applying the positive method of inquiry. Müntz's work rests on acquaintance with original documents: archive papers, memoranda, bills, inventories, and contracts, supported by knowledge of monuments.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-dum:
Francisco Dumetz, a native of Majorca whose birth date is unknown and who died on 14 January 1811. He was the last of the Franciscan friars of California, toiling there without interruption for forty years. He entered the Franciscan order in Majorca and in May 1770 sailed to Mexico with forty-eight other Franciscans for the missionary college of San Fernando in Mexico City. Volunteering for the Indian missions, he was posted to California in October 1770.

Sailing from San Blas with ten friars in January 1771, he arrived at Monterey in May and was assigned to Mission San Diego. He then went to San Carlos in 1772 and San Buenaventura in 1782, where he laboured for the Indians until 1797. Directed to found Mission San Fernando, he stayed there from its founding on 8 September 1797 to the end of 1805, apart from two years at San Gabriel. He served there from 1806 until his death and burial in the church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-von-st:
Johann von Staupitz was the Augustinian leader who first guided Martin Luther and later refused to follow him. Born in Saxony about 1460, he studied at Leipzig, joined the Augustinians, and became prior at Tubingen and doctor of theology in 1500. In 1503 he was elected vicar-general of the German Augustinians and became the first dean of theology at the new University of Wittenberg.

At Erfurt he had consoled the young Luther, tormented by his sinfulness, with talk of God's forgiving grace, and Luther stayed grateful for it. Sent in 1518 to remonstrate with Luther, Staupitz hesitated, released him from obedience to the order, and forwarded his explanation to Rome. When Rome demanded a retraction in 1520, he declared the pope his judge, joined the Benedictines, and ended as Abbot of St. Peter's at Salzburg, Catholic in doctrine to the last.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-maria-:
Joseph Maria von Radowitz was a Prussian general, diplomat, and Catholic statesman. Born at Blankenburg in 1797 of Hungarian descent, he fought with the French in the Wars of Liberation, then served Hesse and, from 1823, Prussia. Raised among Protestants, he became a strong Catholic through study of the Incarnation and the Church's founding.

Rejecting both liberalism and absolutism, Radowitz followed Haller in favoring government by Estates. He improved Prussian artillery, wrote for the Politische Wochenblatt, and served as military attaché at Frankfurt and ambassador to south German courts. After 1840, Frederick William IV often called him to Berlin for advice on German reform.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-caramuel:
Juan Caramuel y Lobkowitz was a Spanish Cistercian prodigy who wrote on nearly everything. Born at Madrid in 1606, he published astronomical tables at ten, learned Asian tongues including Chinese, and joined the Cistercians at La Espina. He earned a Louvain doctorate in 1638, led armed clerics defending Prague from the Swedes in 1648, and ended as Bishop of Vigevano.

Caramuel published, by one count, 262 works on grammar, poetry, mathematics, astronomy, physics, politics, canon law, and theology. Little of it lasts, and his attempt to solve moral theology by mathematical rules won him St. Alphonsus' title Prince of the Laxists. The entry marvels at his range and judges his substance thin.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marie-josephi: A 1913 entry on Goetz — a French writer of note. Janet Stuart lists her works. Little is known of her career. The nineteenth century was her period. The learned press knew her pen. Her 1890 works are famed. Her 1890 writings are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-metz: This 1913 reference piece on Metz — the Moselle diocese. Joseph Lins gives its ancient story. Its bishops guard the river flock. The entry keeps its modest record. A see of the French east. Its 4th-century see is famed. Its bishops are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-olmutz: Olmütz, now Olomouc, became the great Moravian archdiocese with its baroque palaces. This entry covers its archbishops, churches, and history. The faith in Moravia's ancient capital: its archbishops crowned Bohemian kings through the long and storied centuries of Moravian history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-aloys-g: This biographical entry profiles Peter Aloys Gratz, a German biblical scholar of the 1800s, tracing his career, his studies, and his place as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's scholarly gallery, preserved among its German exegetes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-samuel-fritz: Samuel Fritz was the Jesuit of the Amazon. This entry traces his missions, his map, and his fame. The apostle of the Omagua tribes: his great map charted the Amazon in 1691's printing in Quito's press in the Andes of Ecuador.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-arnulf-of-: St. Arnulf was the bishop of Metz. This entry traces his court, his hermitage, and his fame. The ancestor of the Carolingians: his great see crowned Metz in the 610s' Austrasia in the kingdom of the Franks in the north.
nasa-tm-19700002181-snap-8-nak-pump-moto:
Fred Boecker of Lewis Research Center reports start tests for the SNAP-8 sodium-potassium pump motor assembly in this November 1969 memorandum. Two hermetically sealed induction motor pumps were tested in NaK loops. NaK, a sodium-potassium mixture, carries heat in the SNAP-8 space power system.

Tests checked starting on 400-hertz power across wide temperature ranges. Flow resistance was preset by a valve before each start, covering flow rates up to a high maximum. Both pumps started successfully at the hotter stator conditions reported. At colder stator temperatures, both pumps experienced startup difficulties. The pattern tells designers the thermal conditions a SNAP-8 pump needs for reliable starts.
quotes-and-images-from-memoirs-of-cardin:
Quotes and Images from the Memoirs of Cardinal de Retz, prepared by David Widger, lifts short passages from the Cardinal's memoirs and arranges them in alphabetical order. Retz wrote from inside the plots and civil wars of seventeenth-century France, and the extracts carry his cool, worldly voice.

He judged actions by men, the first entries say, and never men by actions, and he sacrificed little affairs to greater ones. Civil war is called a complicated disease, not powerful enough to conclude a peace. Buckingham had been in love with three queens, arms untempered by laws quickly become anarchy, and contempt is named the most dangerous disease of any state.
